title: Don’t Read Old Books. . .Badly
author: John Mark Reynolds
summary: John Mark Reynolds recalls writing an undergraduate paper on a supposed contradiction in Plato and realizing later that his hostile reading ignored three basic facts: Plato was being read in translation, each dialogue is a whole, and a character may use a term in a specialized way. He then applies the same three cautions to the "contradiction mongers" who compile lists of Bible inconsistencies, using the many senses of "just" and "justice" to show how English translation hides differences between Hebrew and Greek terms. The core claim is that reading for errors rather than for meaning is a failure of charity and of scholarship. Reynolds closes with the classical-liberal-arts conviction that a charitable reader can learn goodness, truth and beauty from authors as varied as Russell, Eliot, Hughes and Sayers.
points: Reading an old author to catch contradictions rather than to understand him is an easy undergraduate move, and it produces hostility instead of learning.
Three checks guard against bad reading: remember you are reading a translation, treat each work as a whole before comparing it to others, and expect specialized uses of key terms.
The same checks expose weak apologetics and "Internet atheism" that lift two verses out of different books, languages and eras and call them contradictory.
The many English meanings of "just" illustrate how much scholarship is needed to compare a Hebrew term with a Greek term translated by the same word.
Charity is the precondition of joy in reading: the best reader looks for the best the writer has said and can learn from authors across traditions.
quotes: I was reading for errors, not meaning. Instead of beginning sympathetically, my goal of writing a paper was causing me to read with hostility.
Plato did not write in English. I was reading him in translation, and two different translators had worked on the two dialogues.
Each Platonic dialogue is a whole. Plato does not appear as a character in his own dialogues, so attributing anyone’s views to Plato himself is complicated.
Each Biblical book is a whole and must first be understood for the message it conveys before a “harmony” or contradiction can be found.
The unjust reader quotes only two verses that seem to contradict each other and feels justified in his injustice.
This is tolerable in a kid encountering ancient literature for the first time, but inexcusable in a grown-up who believes he is making a serious argument.
Charity allows me to read a diversity of books and learn from all of them. Authors from Bertrand Russell to TS Eliot to Langston Hughes to Dorothy Sayers can teach me goodness, truth, and beauty.
The bad reader misses all the joy of good reading! Thank God I no longer read for problems but instead read looking for the best the writer has said.
